utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced, but I'd like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draskovic, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text of it is now handed out to you. May I invite to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please slowly give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Gojko Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of March, 1964 in the village of Arazi [phoen], municipality of Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, where did you live until the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo. Ozrenska Street, number 79, municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were you doing before the war broke out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a small business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of military education, training, or perhaps a military rank?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the war broke out, were you politically active?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That year, 1992, did you receive call-up papers? Did you become involved militarily?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the Territorial Defence sent me call-up papers in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, what is this municipality from which you received these call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was this first military assignment of yours and practically what unit did you become a member of?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: My first military assignment was as follows. Practically we who lived in that street organised ourselves and guarded our homes until the Army of Republika Srpska was formed. After the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, we remained in the same place. I was a member of the 3rd Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanized Brigade, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During these first months after the Army of Republika Srpska was established, did you have any kind of position of leadership? Were you an officer or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: At first I was a soldier, a member of the 3rd Platoon, and then towards the end of 1992, I became commander of the 3rd Platoon of the 3rd Company and then towards the end of 1993, I became company commander. And sometime around the end of the war when Dayton was signed I was deputy battalion commander until I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you carried out the duty that you refer to, deputy battalion commander, when the peace agreement was signed, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: One battalion was formed out of two and there was a single command and there was this command of the battalion that tried to take care of all the paperwork for all the soldiers involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you were practically demobilised and when did you stop being a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I think around the middle of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, did you get any kind of military rank or promotion?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, lieutenant. And in 1994, I was in Banja Luka taking a course for battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this military training of yours go on in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: About a month. And over this short period of time, we managed to learn what was important for commanding a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do tell us: During these war years, who were the commanders of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: First it was Captain Stojanovic, who was battalion commander; and after him, Aleksandr Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first name you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Aleksandr Stojanovic -- no Aleksandr Petrovic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the captain you mentioned before what was his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the court who was commander of your brigade during those four years of war?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems there were a lot of Stojanovics in your unit.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the defence area of your battalion, and by way of clarification, because the Court had an opportunity to see these documents what was the right flank of the defence or area of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Vrbanja bridge, or, rather, the Metalija building I think that's what was called. It's been a long time so I have forgotten some things. On the left side there was the barracks, Slavisa Vajner Cica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court how big this is in terms of metre, hundreds of metres or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, say, 3, 3 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This entire area, was it all the urban part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, within that zone, what was the defence area of your company? And do start from the right flank.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The right flank of defence of my unit was the Zeljeznicar stadium or that area, but Moravska and Ozrenska Street, that intersection where these two streets cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your company, did it hold positions in part of Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your company were there other companies within your battalion that practically held positions in Ozrenska Street within their own area of defence?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: There was also the 4th Company, the 5th Company, and the 6th Company that later because there were so few people there, became attached to my unit. That's probably one of the longest streets in Sarajevo and that's why three or four companies had to cover the area of Ozrenska Street which was very densely populated, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't hold this against us. We're just waiting for the interpretation so you don't think it's something else. Obviously both of us are fast speakers, so it takes time. Tell us, during the war did you, with your unit - that is to say, your company - did you have any changes of your initial position in the area of defence?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Practically my company consisted of people who lived in that street. We held positions in front of our own homes and practically we were defending that throughout the war, and that is where we were when Dayton was signed. There weren't any changes except perhaps for some slight changes in the line but that was basically due to engineering works rather than any kind of movement as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your company, during those four years of war, did it receive any orders that had to do with an offensive, in terms of breaking through enemy positions?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Never. Practically we were guarding our own homes. That's where we lived. Our line of defence was in front of our homes. That's where we started the war and that's where we ended the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your company, how many people were there? I understand that this is a category that changes but give us a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: 200 to 250 up to 350 depending on the period involved. There were a lot of combatants there who had been wounded. Some of them were seriously wounded, some of them not so seriously, and then they could not be part of the unit anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many companies did your battalion have?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Our battalion had six companies. I've already said, the 6th Company, towards the end of the war, was attached to the 3rd Company because of the small number of personnel involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us for the sake of precision, if you can remember, when did this reorganisation take place within the battalion; and when was this company attached to the other companies within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was in the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, when I look at the 65 ter witness summary, then I see that the gist of the evidence of this witness would be that this witness and others were sniped at, that were working squads and what kind of vehicles the other parties have. The organisation of his battalion and whether it changed halfway, yes or no, seems to have little or no relevance for what apparently you want to elicit from this witness. So, therefore, I would -- before we go into such details, which seem to be totally foreign to what you want to establish, I urge you to get to the points which, at least on the basis of the 65 ter summary, are the relevant ones. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get to that, Your Honour, just a few more questions by way of a introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we don't need the details as the -- not -- I mean, we've listened to it now for some 15 minutes. All details which, at least I'm unable to link meaningfully with what apparently is the purpose of the calling of this witness. So try to get loose of what you have prepared and come to the relevant points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the intensity of fighting in Ozrenska Street and in the area of defence of your company during those four years of war in view of other parts of the Sarajevo theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Ozrenska Street was certainly one of the most difficult parts of the Sarajevo theatre of war. Practically every day we were exposed to sniping, in particular. Also, the terrain of Ozrenska Street is such that it was hard to protect oneself, especially from snipers. Practically the entire city in front of us and everybody building was a location from which snipers could operate against Ozrenska. If we look at the composition of the company, the average age was 50. People were that age. They had health problems, eyesight problem, hearing problems, so great losses were sustained in Ozrenska Street as I've already said. The battalion covered each and every part of Ozrenska Street, and especially civilians who lived in Ozrenska Street, although there weren't that many of them, were particularly exposed to sniping, to sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have enough fighters to perform the tasks assigned to your unit?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: It depended. As I said already, age was an issue because the average age was 50. There were very few young people, which was particularly aggravating in an area such as Ozrenska Street. There were never enough of people around and we always needed personnel at Ozrenska Street. Whatever people we had, we organised them and put up resistance, defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the front lines of your company and the opposing unit on the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: We were quite close. At times, the distance was 30 metres or 50 metres or just a street in between the houses. The lines were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the positions you held where your defence line was, could you observe the origin of sniping on the positions of your unit?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we certainly could. We observed and monitored the activity of their snipers. The most serious problem we had was a sniping nest at the so-called Milana Pavkovica motel which was put up during the Olympics. It was very close to our positions and we were constantly exposed to sniping from there. There was also another building across the street from the Zeljeznicar football club stadium and another building at Pera Kosorica Square as well as many others. Basically each and every building was suited for sniping purposes but there were some places where we pointed them out more frequently and we tried to neutralise such sniping nests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion, personally, to observe such sniping positions as the officer in the company?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes I was mostly engaged in observing and reconnoitring and I had to be present constantly as the commander together with my fighters. I personally observed and detected sniping positions so as to caution our soldiers and the civilians moving along the Ozrenska Street, to tell them where danger lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court if, during the war years, there were any artillery -- there was any artillery fire from the ABiH against your positions.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There was a war going on. There was constant firing on our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As someone who had the level of military training you had, could you estimate what kind of artillery weapon was used against your positions?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Most frequently they were the 60- and 82-millimetre mortars that were mounted on some vehicles that were in motion and were difficult to detect. They could open fire from the Vaso Miskin Crni factory and the health centre at Malta and some other facilities. As I said, they were mounted on vehicles. They were mobile. And their target -- or their aim was probably to make detection more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the company officer, did you personally observe the artillery positions you described?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We observed constantly at the front line. So as soon as our observers would notice anything, I would go there myself to observe where the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that it was war time, I wanted to ask you whether your company, in its ranks, had artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had 60-millimetre mortars. And as part of the battalion there was a mortar platoon most likely which engaged the enemy. We only had 60-millimetre mortars in our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where the battalion mortars were placed?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Behind our line, in the Prljavo Brdo settlement. To tell you the truth, I don't know where they were exactly because there was no need for me to move there. I was at the lines held by my company and there was no need for me to leave the company sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the company commander, did you, at any point in time, receive any kind of orders that would concern the use of artillery against the positions of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We couldn't engage properly with our 60-millimetre mortar. We used it more at night, to fire signal rockets mostly. The people I had in my company were around 50 years of age so their hearing and eyesight were not so good anymore and whenever they heard or observed anything we would fire signal rockets so that we could try and see whether there was any moving on the other side in the company sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your company have trained sharpshooters and sniping weapons as part of its arsenal?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, if you know, where in Sarajevo was Ivana Krndelja Street. It was so named until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see that street from your company positions in part or as a whole, if at all?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Some parts were visible but most of it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in between. Is it your testimony that you never used your mortars to fire any rounds apart from just to illuminate at night, to be able to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, we did have a 60-millimetre mortar in our company and we used it more at night to fire signal rockets. We did not have any trained crews, of course, and I saw the mortar for the first time when the war began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever fire projectiles not being signal rockets but just to engage the other party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we did, since we had the mortar, we used it to fire other projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you told us a minute ago that you couldn't engage properly with your 60-millimetre mortars, that you used it more at night to fire signal rockets mostly. So -- but you used it to engage the enemy but you often used it at night to fire signal rockets. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at night. I said that we used the mortar most frequently at night to fire signal rockets to illuminate the positions held by our company to control the area. Of course, at times, in day-time, we also used other types of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just mortar bombs if I understand you well, other projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now did you do so at the instruction of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did that when there was any pronounced sniping coming from the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have to correct the transcript. The previous answer, yes, was not given by counsel but by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you -- was there a standing order that you could use your artillery as you wished or as you considered right to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said already, we used it exclusively when there was pronounced sniping against our positions. In that way, we tried to interfere with the activity of snipers in order to protect our soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You only used it against snipers, to eliminate sniper nests or sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because the sniping was our biggest problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, behind your forward positions - so behind your back - was there an elevation held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To our right side, there was Debelo Brdo and to our left there was Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the positions at Debelo Brdo - if you know, given the fact that you hail from the area - could one see Ivana Krndelja Street in part or as a whole?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so because Debelo Brdo is quite high an elevation and I think from that position one can see the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war years, did you - and I have in mind your company - have any POWs?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were civilians crossing the front lines in the area held by your company?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what was going on in that respect and what kind of situation -- situations it entailed.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Often, especially at night, there were people coming from the area of Sarajevo, the part controlled by the ABiH. Civilians were crossing over to our side. There were Serbs and others. It is well-known that a large number of Croats crossed our lines, I think, in 1994. So it frequently happened that civilians came across the lines at night to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you treat such persons under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers standing guard notified the company duty officer who notified the battalion duty officer. They were always taken over by the battalion security officer for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the wartime events, within your defence area, was there any need for pioneering and fortification work at the positions held by your company?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please describe for the Court what kind of pioneer work it engaged. What kind of activity was it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The layout of Ozrenska Street is such that it lies above the settlement of Grbavica making it suitable for sniping from -- by the enemy. Therefore, we were forced to carry out many -- much fortification work. Ozrenska Street is well-known for the number of its embankments. Otherwise one could not move up and down the street. Where there was no shelter, one couldn't move at all especially at day-time. We asked the battalion command to provide equipment for engineering work, and whenever they could, they also assigned people to us from work detachments to come and work on the fortification -- fortifying of our positions. It didn't happen often, but at times only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how frequently did that occur during the war? How often did your company have such needs?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: We had much need for that; but, unfortunately, they did not have enough understanding for it. Perhaps once or twice a month we would receive personnel from the working platoons or civilian protection who worked on fortifying our positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say people from the civilian protection and working squads, please explain the Court how things worked. Who were the people who were engaged in such engineering work?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were people who were not fit to carry arms. They were Bosniaks, Serbs. We asked the battalion command for such people, and they would usually be accompanied by someone who would spend some time there with them. They shared our food. They shared our cigarettes. So in terms of conditions, they were identical to ours. As the company commander, I frequently wished that the roles were reversed, that I could do their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you -- you said they would usually be accompanied by someone who would spend some time there with them. I mean, that's -- if you accompany someone, you spend time with that person. Could you tell us - it's rather vague - what was the role of those accompanying persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the role of these persons was primarily to safe-guard these people. Because Ozrenska Street, along which they were moving, was truly exposed to sniping, so for that reason, there had to be someone who was familiar with the terrain or, rather, the places where there was most sniper fire so the people could safely reach where they were going. And also for the sake of the safety of the person who was guarding them, he stayed in that area where they worked and when they would finish working, then they would return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they have any role in observing whether people would not evade doing what they were supposed to do, so as to be sure that they did the job as they were instructed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, once they would get to the area of the company, they would be told roughly what was supposed to be done, but no one ever insisted that it had to be completed on that day and no one of said how much should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they free to say, Well, I'd rather not go there and do the job.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably people who had health problems could say that and they would certainly be spared on that day or during those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they were obliged to go there? As -- as a principle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was the percentage of Serbs and non-Serbs the same as overall in the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that in the civilian protection and work platoons there were Serbs and Muslims. However, I really don't know about percentages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, at that time of imminent threat of war and in some periods of a state of war, was military call-up obligatory for every military aged able-bodied man?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I guess that's the way it is in any country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Work obligation regarding those who were not fit for military service, was that also obligatory, as the word itself says, in terms of carrying out the state -- the duties assigned by the state?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody had to contribute in some way to the defence of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody would refuse military call-up to report to a war-time unit, would such a person be subjected to a certain responsibility on the basis of the law?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if somebody is not fit for military service for some reason, if a person would refuse to carry out work obligation as assigned by the state, would such a person be subject to responsibility or punishment?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you said that sometimes you wished to take the place of these people, to switch positions. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was exposed day and night to enemy fire. I had to take care of my fighters. I had to take care of the civilian population. Basically the burden of my company was on my shoulders. And these people who came, I had to think about whether food would be provided on time because of the war operations. Sometimes we wouldn't get food on time and then that is why I often thought about them so that somebody else would think of them and providing food for them, and their task was to work on the lines primarily where it was safe, at least to a certain degree. At 3.00, when they finished their work obligation they go home and I continue, day and night, to care about the fighters, what would happen during the night, is whether somebody night be wounded, somebody might be killed, and they didn't have to care about any of that. That is why I thought about that often that I'd like to be in civilian protection, in the work platoon, rather than doing what it was that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there situations within the mentioned engineering works that somebody -- some of the people from civilian protection or, rather, work obligation would fall victim to the sniper fire of Bosnia-Herzegovina or some gun-fire or artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is well-known that snipers would aim at anything that was moving. So there were situations when members of the civilian protection and work platoons would get hit. There were some situations when my soldiers, as they were getting these wounded people out, would get killed. So we were in the same situation, the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about yourself? During the years of war, did you lose any family members due to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my wife's father was hit in the forehead and killed by sniper fire and also uncles, all of them in the area of Vrace, and all of them, right there, at their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of your father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Pandurevic, Nikola Milorad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a soldier or civilian at the time?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a soldier. Although he did not have one eye, he could have been relieved of military obligation, but because of the people who were standing guard there and who were carrying out their duty, he didn't want to miss that. He would often go to the guard post across the street from his house, and he was probably noticed by a sniper and hit and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, if you have information or certain percentages, how many people within your company during those years of war, how many people were killed in combat, how many were killed by sniping, by artillery fire, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: About 300 people were killed, civilians and combatants in Ozrenska Street. I already said that this was a street where the theatre of war was the most difficult in terms of Sarajevo and exposed to sniper fire all the time, and other kinds of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you notice at any point in time from which sniper position this sniper fire came that specifically killed your father-in-law, for instance?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the motel of Milan Pavkovic that was built for the Olympic games. This was a huge fortification. Most of the buildings were made of concrete so this was convenient for snipers, and he was certainly hit from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Motel Pavkovic, until the war was that a military or civilian facility?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian facility that was built for the Olympics in 1984 and it hadn't been completed actually, and I don't think it exists any longer. It was totally destroyed, however, it was torn down after the war. Milan Pavkovic, otherwise, is a well-known painter and photographer and he is from Pofalici otherwise, and probably for the Olympics he got this favourable credit and that is how he started building that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the Pavkovic motel were there residential buildings, family homes, civilian buildings? What kind of neighbourhood is that in Sarajevo where the Pavkovic motel was?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian, houses, densely populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Trg Pera Kosorica, a square from which you noticed sniping fire came. Until the war were there any military facilities there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, since you lived there in that part of Sarajevo, what kind of buildings existed in that square, Pera Kosorica, and what was there purposes?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: These were residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Ozrenska Street, in the defence area of your company, were there any residential buildings in the area of your company or taller buildings or businesses?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Just civilian buildings, individual family homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to your house specifically in Ozrenska Street or, rather, the house of your father-in-law in that street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Still there, but totally destroyed. The walls are there. The roof and everything else was destroyed and unfortunately after the war. Not that much during the war. It was shelled two or three times before the war, but it managed to survive all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, your unit specifically, your battalion, was it fired at from Mojmilo and Debelo Brdo, places that were held by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your knowledge, how much higher is Debelo Brdo in relation to the altitude of the area where your company was?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as the name itself says, Debelo Brdo, Brdo is a hill, it was much higher than Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the last sentence. Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence. Because the interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Debelo Brdo, as the name itself says, is an elevation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Brdo is hill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is much higher than Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Again, we cannot hear the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you again repeat the last part of your sentence. You said it's an elevation. It's much higher than Ozrenska Street. And what did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mojmilo Brdo is a bit higher than Ozrenska Street. Negligibly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time, Your Honour. I know it's the right time to take the break. If you allow me one sentence. I've just received information -- well, after the break, we are going to provide you with a number that we've assigned to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Witness, I'd ask you to follow the usher. We'll take a break for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, Mr. Stojanovic, are you on track, as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And I think it's even going to be shorter because I have refrained from asking some of the questions in view of what you indicated to me, so I think I will need another 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just want to give the number, then we don't need to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But perhaps some of the witnesses whose names I am about to mention may request protective measures. That is why I believe it would be wise to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll do it at the end of this session. Once -- no. The witness may enter the courtroom. We'll do it at the end of the session. Could someone assist the usher in...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, your last answer had to do with Mojmilo hill. I wanted to ask you this: What kind of infrastructure at Mojmilo hill? Was there a facility?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The water supply facility for a part of Sarajevo, was it located close to Ozrenska Street and Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that regard, I wanted to ask you who held the -- that part of the water supply line?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were such facilities on both sides, ours and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible for you and the civilians in Ozrenska Street and that part of Sarajevo to use water if the part of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of BiH did not have any water supply at the same moment?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about gas supply? In terms of supplying it to the part where you lived and the area where the area of defence of your company was, could that part be supplied with gas without the part of Sarajevo controlled by the ABiH being supplied at the same time?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude with the following topic. Because of the intensity of sniping against the positions of your unit and the civilian parts of Ozrenska Street, was it possible to erect certain kind of fortification that would make visibility non-existent from the part held by the members of the army and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have such embankments. Without them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm just concerned that you're testifying not the witness. Instead of putting the question, you're telling the witness why you're putting the question and you're saying to him "because of the intensity of the sniping" instead of the witness telling us what he did and why he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to do so. Thank you for your suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, bearing in mind your previous answer, what kind of obstacles were these?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we usually made them with bricks and mortar but in certain parts, it would require a wall between four and five metres high which was impossible to do. That is why we simply put up some kind of parapets, using blankets and other sorts of material, so as to block the vision of the snipers in the direction of our soldiers and civilians. Without such parapets, it would have been impossible for anyone to move along Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were the dominant buildings in the part of Sarajevo controlled by the ABiH from which one could see even over such obstacles that you have described?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Most apartment buildings could allow for that kind of visibility, especially the four tall high-rises in Pera Kosorica Street and the so-called Loris building across the stadium. Also it was possible to do from some parts of Kupreska Street and my soldiers who were posted at the stadium sustained sniper rifle from that direction. Basically most of any high-rise buildings in that part of Sarajevo were suitable for sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of their use, pre-war use, were those buildings civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, if you could observe that, were civilians living in those same buildings as well?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, during the war years, did you, at any point in time, receive as the company commander any kind of order from your superior command to target civilian facilities from which there was no engaging on the part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find yourself in a situation that certain parts of your positions were monitored by members of the international community, such as UNPROFOR, the UN, or UNMO?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, they were on Borivoje Jeftic Street, there were UN observers there and we co-operated excellently with them. Many of them I still remember some even by first and last name. I think there was a Spanish man by the name of Jimenez, who was the head of mission at Grbavica. He frequently arrived and we always worked together very well. We did not have any problems with any observation mission when it comes to my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the company did you, at any point in time, receive any kind of suggestion or objection by members of the observation missions, in terms of any military activity in Sarajevo or against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Dayton Accords were signed, and bearing in mind that you were still in military engagement for another six months, which entity, the part of Sarajevo where the defence area of your company, had that part?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the Dayton Accords, it was held by the VRS, but the Dayton Accord seized that part, so to speak, and it was made part of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the pre-war population return to that part of Sarajevo, and these days who lives in that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: In Vrace and Ozrenska Street, defended by my company, there were Serb civilians. They are no longer there. It is mostly inhabited by Bosniaks and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with your property in Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The house still exists. It is devastated, for the most part. It was shelled on a few occasions in the war, but the walls are still there and the foundations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, I'd like to thank you on behalf of Mr. Mladic's Defence team and these would be the questions I had of you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draskovic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton, who apparently is ready to do so. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you understand me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. What I'd like to do as we start up is get you to just to confirm a couple of details about your service with the Army of Republika Srpska. First, at temporary page 4 today, you talked about receiving your call-up papers in April 1992. Now to be perfectly clear, you received those Territorial Defence call-up papers from the staff of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Novo Sarajevo municipality was ruled by the SDS after the first pre-war multi-party elections. So it was our municipality, Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, again, just to get some history perfectly straight, your battalion, in fact, was formed as a unit of the VRS in May of 1992 - you said that - and until May of 1993, it was part of the 1st Romanija Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you -- and it was only in May 1993 that it became part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Also correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before Stojanovic, who you talked as your battalion commander, your first battalion commander was actually Brane Pokalovic [phoen]; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Pokalovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your battalion had two deputy commanders. One was Dragan Siljak and the other one was Milan Hrvacevic and Hrvacevic was eventually replaced in 1995 by Bozo Tomic. That's also correct; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as I understand your description of the line that your company manned, That was a stretch of about 900 metres in Grbavica 2, right? It was about 900 metres long.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your line was in the immediate vicinity of the police school in Vrace. That was one of your jobs, was to defend the police school; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in depth of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's where the headquarters of the RS MUP was for a period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And also in your vicinity, although not quite immediately, were the sky-scrapers at Soping where you had the headquarters of your battalion's 2nd Company; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the 2nd Company. Yes, of our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now to go on to the subject of some of the weapons that you talked about with my colleague, you mentioned your battalion's mortars on Prljavo Brdo, and I think you can confirm to me that these were 82-millimetre mortars, can't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there were six of them; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never visited the sector where the mortars were. I was a commander of an infantry company, spending my time in company territory, save for the very few occasions when I went to visit my family, when I left the defence lines of my company.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's talk then about the 60-millimetre mortars your company had. You actually had at least two, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where was that? Was that near the stadium or was it by your company headquarters? Or was it over by the police school? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: It was up there where the 3rd Platoon of my company was, in the part of Ozrenska Street which presented the most difficult part of the front line held by my company.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So was that near your company headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the HQ of the company was in Banja Lucka Street across the street from the police school in the so-called Pajaco restaurant at the beginning of the Ozrenska Street and the mortar was placed where the command of the 3rd Platoon of my company was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it never had to move much, did it, it was stationery effectively?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it correct also, isn't it, that you had a 76-millimetre mountain gun on Kupreska Street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now what about some APCs? They wouldn't have necessarily been your company's materiel. They would have been manned by soldiers from your brigade's mechanised battalion. How many were in your area?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a separate unit. I really did not have any say in where they were going or where they fired from. There were usually two or three in the company sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. And one was on Ozrenska Street; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one was in the immediate vicinity of the police school?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps at times, but I don't know of it being there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you had one above the stadium?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps occasionally to engage from there, but it wasn't above the stadium all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind of guns did these APCs have on them?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: They had 20- or 30-millimetre cannons. I don't know what calibre precisely. And they also probably had the Malyutka self-guiding missiles. I don't know if it was all of them but some of them did have them. It was not in my unit and there was no need for me to know what they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand. Now, just in terms of your unit you also had some machine-gun, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: There must have been some machine-guns but I don't know how many. There was probably the so-called 84 machine-gun and perhaps the M52.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the M84 shoots 7.62-millimetre bullets; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. Really, I cannot remember. It's been 20 years so I've forgotten. I was forced into being a soldier. I don't have any military training. There was no need for me to remember the calibre and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fair enough. But do you remember -- you must have had a couple of machine-guns at the stadium; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: We did. I don't know if there were a couple, but, at the stadium, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one above the stadium in Sanac?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have some in some of those private houses were talking about on Ozrenska Street also; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to go to sort of take a step back now from your company's area of responsibility and to talk about some assets that were controlled by the brigade, the name mechanised brigade means that your brigade had mechanised units so we've already talked about the APCs. They also had a tank unit, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they had some tanks in the area of Grbavica and Vrace; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, tell me if I've got this right. There was one that stayed pretty much around the outpatient clinic in Lenjinova Street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. But that's not the area of responsibility of my company so I don't know the deployment in Grbavica where different weapons were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, for sure you would know about the ones that were moving up and down the transit road; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about some movements. These are such strong engines that anybody would have to hear that, but where they were, ultimately I didn't make any decisions in terms of where these vehicles should go, so I'm really not aware of any of these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I completely accept that you were outside of the decision-making process in terms of the tanks. I have no problem with that. I'm just asking about their locations. There was -- do you remember there was one on Radnicka Street as well; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember one on Bana Surbata Street?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, especially now that I've confused some of these streets because before the war there was one name and then after the war there were other names, so probably I get confused with these street names. But I don't remember this at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, that's fine. And I'm always trying to use the old names so as to avoid any confusion because I recognise that that's kind of difficult to follow. Now, my colleague also asked you whether your company had trained sharpshooters and sniping weapons as part of its arsenal, and that was at temporary page 12 today. But you can confirm -- you said no. But you could also confirm that your battalion had a unit of sharpshooters of about 12 people, and they weren't attached to a particular company. They were under battalion command; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And their job was to operate throughout the battalion's area of responsibility as needed and requested; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly they were within the battalion. They got their assignments through the battalion. I mean, in the company, I did not have a sniper. And it's the battalion that was in charge of these snipers. So it is they who followed where it was that they were being placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they were placed sometimes in the vicinity of your company, though, nevertheless. They would go up to firing positions in the Soping sky-scrapers; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I really don't have that information because they were not duty-bound to report to me, and platoon commanders, probably they were sent by their commanders to certain areas, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're invited to tell us what you observed, so whether you're responsible, whether you had any position to give orders, that's a different matter. So, therefore, the question also includes: Did you see any of that from the Soping sky-scrapers, entering, being in the position, firing from there, did you ever see such a thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Soping sky-scrapers are not in the territory of my company, so I really did not -- I mean, I've already said there a few times. I did not move out of the defence area of my company. I was commander of an infantry company. I was with my soldiers. I have taken an oath here to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I have been acting accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ever seen such activity at Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about -- you talked about elevations to a certain extent today in your testimony in-chief. And you said -- my colleague asked you: "Were the dominant buildings on the part of Sarajevo," at transcript page 26, "... controlled by the ABiH from which one could see over such obstacles." And in that context he was -- or you were referring to something that would block sniping from the Bosnian side. And you said: "Most apartment buildings," referring to those buildings which were within Bosnian-held Sarajevo, "... and the so-called Loris building," you said "most apartment buildings could allow for that and the so-called Loris building across the stadium." But I just want to ask a question about elevations here. The Loris building was immediately opposite the stadium at the same elevation of the stadium, and Ozrenska Street and Vrace where you were talking about are far away above the stadium and above the Loris building; isn't that right? Because you're not trying to tell us that from the Loris building you could see over the top of any barricades to block line of sights on Ozrenska Street, are you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. The last part, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. From the Loris building, you're not saying that anybody could see over the top of any barricades that had been placed on Ozrenska Street to block line of sight, are you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: The Loris building was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's opposite the stadium of Zeljeznicar, that football club and, of course, of it a convenient spot for sniping. How much Ozrenska Street could be seen from there, I really cannot say. I was not in that position but rather on the other side. We made different kinds of shelters made of canvas, bricks, whatever else, so that we could move more easily especially during the day, and night.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, actually, when it comes to any comments about what potential line of sight might be from Bosnian-held territory, you actually haven't been there so you can't speak to line of sight at the time, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know where the snipers were following.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is not... the question is not specific. It doesn't say which building and that creates confusion. Does the Prosecutor mean the Loris building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. No, it's about from any point from Bosnian-held territory. That's what the question is about. If it's not specific then it covers that whole and whether that gives a good chance to an answer that makes sense a different matter. I leave it -- the objection is denied, but that doesn't mean that a rephrasing of the question might not assist. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll actually just move on. I'm quite fine with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You outlined at the beginning of your evidence in-chief the area of responsibility of your battalion. So you were talking about the situation through Grbavica 1 and further onto the east. And because you appear to be able to speak about the situation in your battalion's area of responsibility and we've done that in some detail, I just want to ask you about some firing positions in that area. All right? We've talked about Soping, and I want to move further to the east. You can confirm for us that your battalion had firing positions in the sky-scrapers on what was Lenjinova Street and is now Grbavicka those are the white ones. 4, 6, 6A, 8 and 14A. You can confirm that; right.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the line of another company. I mean, I was in the area of Grbavica very rarely expect for the part that was covered by my company. The Zeljeznicar stadium to the left and right, Ozrenska Street, Ozrenska Street rather was the area of responsibility of my company and that's where I spent most of my time. As for those sky-scrapers, I really don't know those skyscrapers. They were dominant, they were nearby, and near the lines of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak at a slower pace. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to intervene already a couple of times. Could you please slow down in speaking because otherwise some of your words would be lost and we would regret that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So could you -- actually, the witness wasn't given an opportunity to finish his sentence. Perhaps -- well, he was given an opportunity. Perhaps he could repeat it. You said "they were dominant, they were nearby and near the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Would you like to finish your sentence for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not receive a interpretation of this last speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last question, I take it. Could you repeat your question, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We were talking about firing positions and I asked you to confirm your battalion's firing positions in the sky-scrapers on what was Lenjinova Street and what's now Grbavicka Street and I gave you the building numbers the address numbers of those buildings. Can you confirm those firing positions for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I understood the last question to be whether the witness would finish his answer. Because most of it is already on the record. You said, as a latter part of your answer "they were dominant. They were nearby and near the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." What did you add or was that the end of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Soping skyscrapers were really dominant and they were close to the line of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was senseless to make sniper nests because ordinary weapons could be used especially because it was dangerous. Because these sky-scrapers were dominant and even for those who were firing, that would constitute a danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that there were no firing positions in Soping?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had to be that way because there was a war going on, so I really cannot say what are the dominant positions where the positions were. It was an area of another -- of another company so I had no need to go to the area of another company because I was busy enough as it was in my own company.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer is you can't confirm one way or another. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I never entered these sky-scrapers, not during the war, not before the war, not after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now you also talked in your evidence in-chief about these mortars, 60- and 82-millimetre mobile mortars that you said were used by the Bosnian forces. Now my question to you, since you raised it, is: You fired back; right? Because why else would you be raising this evidence? You talked about the mobile mortars, so you fired back at them; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That's only logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you fired back at them with mortars; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when our observers would notice firing from their mortar, especially if they would see where it was coming from, we'd inform the battalion command and then through the mortar platoon, they would fire at those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how long -- but you explained to us that these mobile mortars are extremely difficult to see; right? So how quickly would they move before you were able to fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we invite the witness to answer that question, could I seek one clarification, especially in light of where you said, "before you were able to fire." Did I understand you well that you didn't use your own mortar but that it was sent to the higher levels so that the mortar platoon would engage the mobile mortars from the ABiH side or did you use your own mortar to engage them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a 60-millimetre mortar and its capacities are probably limited. Of course, we could inform the battalion command and the battalion command would use the mortar platoon to fire at these positions where our observers had observed fire from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you didn't use your own mortar for those purposes. You reserved that to engaging sniper positions. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I was a bit uncertain about the "you," whether that would be the mortar platoon or the platoon of which the witnesses was a member. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how quickly would they move before the battalion would respond, before the mortar unit would fire? Because the process that you'd have to go through involves some delay; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Well, our observers usually observed them at night-time. One would see the light, and that's how they could see it. They were usually on vehicles, some vehicles of two tonnes. These are smaller vehicles and, of course, they were on vehicles so that they could fire from different places fast. We would let the battalion command know and then, through the mortar platoon, they would act, and even if they were not there, then we would let them know that we had seen them and that we would fire too. We want to make it known that we have discovered their positions, although they would usually change their positions quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you say "and that we would fire too" or that "they would fire too"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We and they. They fire, we see them. After that, we fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you let them know you see them by firing into the empty space where they were; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment we don't know whether it's an empty space or whether they are still there or whether they had moved. Most often they would move using that vehicle, but I've already said that we did that in order to make it known that we have seen them and that therefore we would fire at the location from which they had fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So the point of firing at that location irrespective of whether or not they were there was to do something like intimidate them into stopping, I suppose; right? Because they're almost impossible to hit otherwise.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was hard to hit them, but let's take it that way. Our mortars would, say, intimidate them, or warn them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just relating to how you used your mortars vis-à-vis snipers on Bosnian side, your evidence is that you would use your mortars against residential buildings from which Bosnian forces were firing; correct? You would use your 60-millimetre mortars against residential buildings to eliminate the snipers. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most often our 60-millimetre mortar would fire from the Pavkovic motel. It was built using concrete. It was huge. And our fighters and the civilian population were affected by that, and, of course, we would fire in order to make it known to that sniper there that we had discovered him. It is impossible to take that. Whoever has not experienced this, is it so hard to describe the feeling of being under sniper fire. You know that the Majmunovic family, people who lived there, even their cow was hit. The sniper shooter killed everyone, including that cow, and that practically paralysed life in Ozrenska Street, and we were trying to deal with it in everyone conceivable way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could I ask your attention for page 43, lines 14 and 15 especially the word "from" which seems rather illogical in this context. And, second, Mr. Stojanovic did not take the effort to locate the Pavkovic motel. If you would do it for him and for yourself, then at least the Chamber would know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I could make an effort to do that over the next break, Your Honour, which I see by the clock is imminent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I had in five minutes on my mind but if you'd rather take the break now then ... But could you already resolve the line where it says "well, most often and I think it would mean our 60-millimetre mortar would fire from the Pavkovic motel ..." I take it it was firing at the Pavkovic motel. Is that what you said, Witness, or did you say that it would fire from the Pavkovic motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the motel. There were snipers active in the motel on the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that has been clarified. Ms. Edgerton, would you like to fill the next three minutes or would you like to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I can fill it, Your Honours and then come back to you on the question of the Pavkovic motel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would continue for another three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mentioned the Pavkovic motel earlier in your testimony but you mentioned other locations including apartment buildings. So my question to you is that - and I'll direct you to that passage in your testimony - it's at temporary page 26 -- pardon me. You were referring to the four tall high-rises in -- and I'm not sure which street you indicated, "the so-called Loris building, parts of Kupreska Street and high-rise buildings." And my colleague asked you: "In terms of their pre-war use, were those buildings civilian or military? " And these are the -- and you indicated they were all civilian buildings. And then my colleague said: "During the war, if you can observe that, were civilians living in those same buildings as well? " And you said: Yes. So just so I get this completely straight. So your evidence is to eliminate Bosnian snipers you fired mortars on buildings where civilians -- where you knew where civilians were living; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. They engaged us the most from the Pavkovic motel and the high-rises at Pera Kosorica square and the Loris building in Kupreska Street where our civilians lived. Their sniping activity was pronounced the most there. Of course, wherever we could observe a sniper we tried to neutralised it, but it is difficult to target a building with a mortar, especially if one is targeting a sniping nest. That is why we tried to neutralise the Pavkovic motel nest which was the closest to our line and caused most trouble for us. Of course, when they fired from the high-rises and the Loris building, we did our utmost to use our machine-guns and infantry weapons to neutralize or intimidate the sharpshooters. As I said it is difficult to target a building with a mortar, especially if one is targeting a sniping location.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you fired on the sky-scrapers in the Pero Kosoric square with tanks as well; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tanks positioned in Vrace and Grbavica operating throughout that area fired on -- putting aside -- I've already said, I accept that you have nothing to do with the chain of command involving the deployment of those tanks. But the tanks positioned in Vrace and Grbavica fired on the skyscrapers at Pera Kosorica Square; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DRASKOVIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I've used up my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've used your three minutes. Where are we in terms of timing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You may in a second. As far as timing is concerned, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll finish in advance of my estimate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wanted to say something, Witness, Mr. Draskovic. Witness -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to mention the tanks engaging Vrace and the high-rises. If someone is targeting you from a high-rise, what else can you do than to defend yourself and try to neutralize it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
